name: Hassan Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mondays and Wednesdays are lab days, which I love, even though I smell of disinfectant by lunch. Tuesdays and Thursdays are lectures in cell biology and statistics, and I'm in the library with a coffee between them. I share a flat above a kebab shop with two lads from my course. Friday and Sunday mornings I make flat whites at the campus café, which pays for my phone and my football boots.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I'm finally working out how the body actually runs. It's like learning the rules of a game I've watched my whole life. What wears me out is statistics, honestly, and being broke by the third week of every month. My dad drives a city bus and he's the union rep for his depot, so the cost of everything is dinner-table talk at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news and a bit funny. We spent years being told our jobs were gone, and it's a tidy little assistant. At the café the till already suggests drinks, and honestly it hasn't changed my shift at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I can relax a bit and just get on with my degree. A biomedical degree leads to lab work, and I think labs will always want people who can handle samples and think. My worry in this picture is the usual one, that there are more graduates than lab jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep the café job, keep studying, and use my summer to try for a placement at the hospital lab, which a few seniors on my course got last year. I'd also start doing the statistics practice questions early, so I'm not panicking in exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty comfortable, to be honest. It feels like a normal year with a normal amount of stress. The kind of worry I can solve with a timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned more graduates than lab jobs. How does that sit with feeling comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You mentioned more graduates than lab jobs. How does that sit with feeling comfortable?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my plan covers it. If the lab route is tight, I can go into medical sales or a masters. And I'd still have my family's help for at least three years. If I thought the whole thing was falling apart I'd say so. Dad always says to worry only about what you can actually change, and I can change my grades.

say: I'd say it's **good news** and a bit funny, after years of being told jobs were gone.
I'd tell the café crew the till suggesting drinks **hasn't changed** my shift.
think: Labs will always want people who can **handle samples** and think.
My only worry is more graduates than lab jobs, which a **placement** can fix.
do: **Keep** the Friday and Sunday café shifts and my degree routine.
**Apply** for a hospital lab placement next summer, like two seniors did.
**Start** statistics practice questions early, so exams don't cause panic.
feel: **Comfortable**, like a normal year with a normal amount of stress.
S0.quote: Dad always says to worry only about what you can actually change, and I can change my grades.
fieldNote: Hassan is **genuinely settled** here; his family help and a plan B make the plateau comfortable.
He uses his dad's **union rep** philosophy as a steadying line.
He leans on **practical** timetables, not big beliefs, to handle stress.

steps.text: Keep the Friday and Sunday café shifts
Apply for a summer placement at the hospital lab
Practise statistics questions every week from January

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should expect the boring parts of jobs to go first, and be honest about who gets the benefit. Writing reports, booking, checking: those go to software. If that's what it does to office staff, my mum, who's a school receptionist, will notice before I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree is a good one for that world because lab work needs hands and judgement. But the thinking part of my degree, like analysing results, might be done by software before I graduate. So I'd need to be the person who can check what the software says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools properly, not just now and then. I'd try the ones my lab tutor recommends for data analysis, and I'd do it with a friend so we compare notes. I'd also join the student union's jobs forum, because they run workshops with local firms. And I'd keep my café shifts to have an income that isn't a screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled but curious. I like that I'm young enough to pick up the new stuff, but I'd feel a bit sorry for people who've done the same job for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change about how you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would change about how you study?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read the paper first, then ask the software to check my reasoning, not the other way round. If I let it do the thinking, I won't know when it's wrong, and in a lab being wrong costs real money. I'd want my tutors to tell us which parts we must do by hand. Right now nobody says.

say: I'd say **boring parts** of jobs go first, and we should be honest about who benefits.
I'd say my mum's **school office** will notice the change before I do.
think: Lab work needs **hands and judgement**, but analysing results may be done by software.
I'd need to be the person who can **check** what the software says.
do: **Use** the data analysis tools my lab tutor recommends, with a friend.
**Join** the student union jobs forum for workshops with local firms.
**Keep** my café shifts as income that isn't a screen job.
feel: **Unsettled but curious**, and a bit sorry for people thirty years into one job.
S1.quote: I'd read the paper first, then ask the software to check my reasoning, not the other way round.
fieldNote: He sees the tools as **useful if checked**, which fits his steady, proof-first outlook.
His worry points to **others** (mum, long-serving workers), not himself.
He wants tutors to say what must be **done by hand**, a gap he's noticed.

steps.text: Learn the data analysis tools my lab tutor recommends
Join the student union jobs forum
Keep the café shifts as a non-screen income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments and universities need to say out loud what they are doing, because two years leaves no space for slow reports. I'd tell my friends it's not the time to drop a degree, but also that nobody can honestly promise a safe path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm rattled. By 2028 I'd be in my third year, about to look for a graduate job, and thinking jobs, like entry-level data and lab analysis roles, would already be going. Dad drives a bus, so he'd have until about 2031, but Mum's school office job would be hit first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about what we'd do if both their incomes wobble. I'd get serious about the hands-on side of my degree, like lab techniques that robots find harder, and try for as much practical experience as possible. I'd also take more café shifts and save, and I'd ask Dad's union if there's a plan, because they negotiate for the drivers' jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a heavy feeling, like being on a bus that's speeding up and nobody has told you the route. I'd still have laughs with the lads, but at night I'd be calculating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the plan look like if neither parent could help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would the plan look like if neither parent could help?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the union do, in a world like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move back home and drop to a part-time course, if the university allows it. I'd work full-time at the café or a warehouse until I knew what jobs there were. It would be a year lost, but a year lost is better than ten thousand pounds of extra debt for a degree nobody values. I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

say: I'd say **nobody** can honestly promise a safe path, and slow reports won't do in two years.
I'd tell friends not to **drop** their degree out of panic.
think: Entry-level data and lab analysis jobs could be **going** by the time I graduate.
Mum's school office job would be hit **first**, and Dad's bus a few years later.
do: **Talk** with my parents about what we'd do if both incomes wobble.
**Seek** extra hands-on lab practice and take more café shifts to save.
**Ask** Dad's union what plan exists for drivers.
feel: Like a bus **speeding up** with nobody telling you the route.
S2.quote: A year lost is better than ten thousand pounds of extra debt for a degree nobody values. I'd hate it, but I'd do it.
fieldNote: The **household earners** are what push him to anxious; he's not alarmed because he keeps a plan.
His fallback plan is **practical and sad**: part-time study, full-time work.
He wants **hands-on** skills as a hedge, showing he's absorbed the exposure idea.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents and plan for two lost incomes
Book extra practical lab sessions in the holidays
Take two more café shifts a month
Ask Dad's union what plan exists for drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a clever plan if people are honest. I'd say it at the student union, because they could bargain with firms now for graduate paths, before the jobs vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be okay. I'd graduate in 2029, with two years before AI can do almost any thinking work. If I get into a lab, hands-on lab work should last until robots arrive in 2034. My mum's job is the risk, and I'd want her to start planning early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for a hospital lab job with a clear training track, and I'd do a masters part-time if I could. I'd also be learning AI tools weekly, so I'm the one who checks them. And I'd help Mum look at courses, maybe in school administration software or teaching assistant work, because those are close to what she knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A five-year warning feels like a hill, not a wall. I'd be more motivated than scared. I'd have a bit of a knot in my stomach about Mum, but that's okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum think about changing jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does your mum think about changing jobs?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you put your effort first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she's too old at fifty-two, and then she'd say it again at dinner. But she runs the whole school office, so she's got skills that matter. I'd show her that courses can be online and cheap, and I'd offer to sit with her for the first lesson. If that doesn't work, I'd at least make sure we have a plan B.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** for a clever plan if everyone is honest.
I'd push the student union to **bargain** with firms for graduate paths now.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 and have **two years** before thinking AI is that strong.
Hands-on lab work should last until **robots** arrive around 2034.
do: **Aim** for a hospital lab job with a clear training track.
**Learn** AI tools weekly, so I'm the one who checks them.
**Help** Mum find cheap online courses near her school office skills.
feel: **Manageable**, like a hill not a wall, with a small knot about Mum.
S3.quote: A five-year warning feels like a hill, not a wall. I'd be more motivated than scared.
fieldNote: Hassan's **steady** temperament shows: time turns fear into a to-do list.
His concern is **Mum**, and he plans to sit beside her on day one of a course.
He treats AI tools as a **checking skill**, consistent with his earlier answer.

steps.text: Aim for a hospital lab job with a training track
Learn AI tools weekly so I can check their results
Help Mum find cheap online courses
Study a part-time masters if a lab offers support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and that we should stop treating this like a disaster movie. I'd say unions and universities should use the time to build proper retraining, and I'd say it at the dinner table to Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel okay. By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine with a career underway, and my parents would be close to retirement. I'd be a bit worried about whether the pension holds, but that's a different problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my degree, then a lab job, and I'd use the extra years to learn something that sits alongside it, like data and programming. I'd also start saving into a pension from my first pay cheque. And I'd probably volunteer with Dad's union, because by then there'll be a lot of members who need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit curious. If it works out well, it could even make my work more interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who's panicking about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who's panicking about it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change your calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to put the phone down and look at the calendar. Ten years is longer than school and university put together. You can learn a whole second profession in that time. Panic is a bad planner, and I'd rather be a boring planner.

say: I'd say stop treating this like a **disaster movie** and build proper retraining.
I'd tell Dad over dinner that unions can **use** these years.
think: By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine, with a **career** underway and parents near retirement.
The bigger worry is whether the **pension** holds, which is a different problem.
do: **Study** data and programming alongside my lab career.
**Pay** into a pension from my first pay cheque.
**Volunteer** with Dad's union to help members who need retraining.
feel: **Calm** and a bit curious; it could even make my work more interesting.
S4.quote: Ten years is longer than school and university put together. You can learn a whole second profession in that time.
fieldNote: The long runway lets Hassan's **planner** side dominate; he's honestly calm.
He sees **pensions**, not jobs, as the real remaining risk.
His **union volunteering** idea comes from home, not from the course.

steps.text: Learn data analysis and programming next to my degree
Start a pension payment from my first paycheque
Volunteer with Dad's union to help members retrain

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It leaves no time to change course, and it hits Mum's office job first. What would help is real information from the university about which careers last, a retraining fund for people like my parents, and honest plans from the government. Even a clear date for when it will be updated would be useful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that a lot of students my age are quietly working out plan Bs, and we'd like adults to take us seriously. We aren't all glued to our phones.

headlineQuote: A lot of students my age are quietly working out plan Bs, and we'd like adults to take us seriously.
portrait: Hassan is **nineteen**, studying biomedical science, living above a kebab shop with two course mates and working at a campus café.
He is **progressive**, shaped by a bus-driver dad who is a union rep and a mum in a school office.
He is steady and practical, so he tests new tools once they are **proven** and always checks their work.
He stays calm in slow worlds and becomes **anxious** when his parents' incomes are at stake.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because it leaves no time to change course and hits Mum first.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **information** from the university about which careers last, plus a retraining fund for people like his parents.
